OVERLAP WITH 65/3/1 IS MASSIVE, AND CONTRADICTS THE BRIEFING I WAS GIVEN. I was told this series' sets are 'genuinely DIFFERENT papers, not permutations' and that plan.txt's 3-covered/40-new split meant the questions really differ. That is FALSE for 65/3/3 against 65/3/1: matching on CONTENT, 41 of my 54 rows are the same question as a 65/3/1 row, merely renumbered and reshuffled. Only 13 are genuinely new (Q3, Q5, Q8, Q10, Q12, Q14, Q22, Q23, Q28, Q30 (a), Q30 (b), Q33, Q34). plan.txt under-detects because the marking scheme RE-TYPESETS the blocks between sets, so byte-hashing fails on questions that are word-for-word identical — exactly the caution in §6 of the brief. Its own attributions are also unreliable here: it claims 'Q6 ~ 65-3-1 Q3' when my Q6 is 65/3/1's Q2, and 'Q25 ~ 65-3-1 Q30' when my Q25 is 65/3/1's Q24.
METHOD, per §6's recommended path: for all 41 overlapping rows I read the question on MY page first, confirmed it matched, and only then reused 65/3/1's stem / option / context text byte-for-byte, so the whole sitting is reconstructible from this file and the rows still dedup at commit. The map (mine → 65/3/1's) is Q1→Q15, Q2→Q16, Q4→Q18, Q6→Q2, Q7→Q3, Q9→Q5, Q11→Q7, Q13→Q9, Q15→Q11, Q16→Q12, Q17→Q13, Q18→Q14, Q19→Q19, Q20→Q20, Q21a/b→Q25a/b, Q24a/b→Q23a/b, Q25→Q24, Q26→Q31, Q27a/b→Q26a/b, Q29a/b→Q28a/b, Q31→Q30, Q32a/b→Q35a/b, Q35a/b→Q34a/b, Q36*→Q38*, Q37*→Q36*, Q38*→Q37*.
⚠ THE CASE-STUDY NUMBERING IS PERMUTED, which is the hazard §5 warns about: my Case Study – 1 (triangular park) is 65/3/1's Case Study – 3; my – 2 (light poles) is its – 1; my – 3 (dropout survey) is its – 2. The passages are byte-identical; only `_caseStudyLabel` differs, and that label is deliberately kept OUT of `context`.

MEASURED FACTS FOR THIS PAPER: option labels print UPPERCASE (A) (B) (C) (D) throughout — paper, Hindi pages and marking scheme alike. Case-study headings ARE printed and use an EN DASH: 'Case Study – 1' (Hindi 'प्रकरण अध्ययन – 1'). DECIMAL STYLE REMAINS UNMEASURED for this series: like 65/3/1, this paper prints NO decimal number anywhere — the only non-integers are fractions and percentages (40%, 5%, 10%, 90%). The 2026 text layer is glyph-encoded and unusable; everything here was read from the rendered images.

CBSE DEFECTS FOUND — see the `_flag` on Q33 (CBSE's own marking scheme rules the question is not a function and awards full marks for attempting), and on Q24 (a) / Q24 (b) (printing defects inherited from 65/3/1 and re-verified on my pages). One further MARKING-SCHEME defect that touches no question row and so carries no flag: Sol. 34 (ms page idx 13) heads its corner-point table 'Value of Z=600x+400y' while the question maximises Z = 8x + 8y. The five tabulated values (160, 320, 360, 320, 0) are all correct for 8x + 8y, so the header alone is wrong — and 600x + 400y is precisely the objective of 65/3/1's Q33, confirming the scheme was assembled by copy-paste from the sibling set.

questions._flag: Bracketing transcribed EXACTLY as printed (paper page idx 12, marking scheme ms page idx 7): 'sin [cot^-1 √2 (cos (tan^-1 1))]', with no bracket grouping the √2 with the cos factor, so read literally the √2 sits outside cot^-1's argument. RESOLVED, and by CBSE rather than by us: Sol. 24(a) works it as sin[cot^-1 √2 (cos π/4)] = sin(cot^-1 1) = sin π/4 = 1/√2, i.e. the √2 IS inside — \(\sin[\cot^{-1}(\sqrt{2}\cos(\tan^{-1}1))]\). Identical defect to 65/3/1 Q23 (a), the same typeset block reused.

questions.stem: A relation R on \(A = \{1, 2, 3\}\) is defined as \(R = \{(1, 1)\ (3, 3), (1, 2)\}\). Is R a symmetric relation ? Justify. Write the smallest relation set \(R_1\) such that \(R \cup R_1\) becomes an equivalence relation on the set \(\{1, 2, 3\}\).
questions._flag: PRINTING DEFECT, transcribed as printed: the relation set carries NO comma between the first two pairs — '{(1, 1) (3, 3), (1, 2)}' — in the English (page idx 12), the Hindi (page idx 11) AND the marking scheme's own reprint (ms page idx 7), so it is CBSE's, not a transcription slip. The three pairs are unambiguous and the official answer (R is not symmetric since (1,2) is in R but (2,1) is not; \(R_1 = \{(2,2), (2,1)\}\)) reads them exactly that way. Opposite sides of a square are along the lines :

\(\vec{r} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - 4\hat{k} + \lambda(2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 6\hat{k})\)

\(\vec{r} = 3\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - 5\hat{k} + \mu(2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 6\hat{k})\)

Show that a function \(f : R_+ \to A \subset N\), defined as \(f(x) = 4x^2 + 12x + 15\) is one-one. Find set A so that f is onto where \(R_+ = [0, \infty)\). Also, find if there exists \(a \in R_+\) such that \(f(a) = 7\). Justify.
questions._flag: CBSE'S OWN MARKING SCHEME DECLARES THIS QUESTION DEFECTIVE. Sol. 33 (ms page idx 13) reads, in full: 'f defined in the question is not a function. So, full marks to be given for attempting the question.' — 5 marks, unconditionally. The defect is the codomain: for any non-integer \(x \in R_+\) (e.g. \(x = 0{\cdot}5\) gives 22, but \(x = 1/3\) gives \(19\tfrac{8}{9}\)) the value \(4x^2 + 12x + 15\) is not a natural number, so no subset A of N can receive f and the map is not well defined. Stem transcribed exactly as printed; there is no correct answer to author, and any later solution step should record CBSE's ruling rather than attempt the question.

Two vertical light poles of height 22 m and 16 m stand on the opposite sides of a 20 m wide road as shown below in the figure.

Two ladders of length \(l_1\) and \(l_2\) are placed from a common point R on the road at a distance of x m from the smaller pole.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
questions._figure: REQUIRED — the schematic the stem points at ('as shown below in the figure'). It is what fixes the arrangement the stem only half-states: pole AB (22 m) on the left, pole CD (16 m) on the right, the 20 m road as BD, R a point of BD with x measured from D (the shorter pole), ladder \(l_1\) from R to A and \(l_2\) from R to C. questions.stem: Find the probability that a student selected at random is a regular student.
questions.context:
A survey was conducted to find out the success rate of students who qualified the entrance examination by dropping a year after class XII.

As per the data collected, 40% students appearing in the examination were dropouts and the remaining students were regular students of class XII.

Of the dropouts, 5% qualify the examination while 10% of the regular students qualify the examination.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions.
questions._figure: DECORATIVE — a cartoon of a student at a desk piled with books under a thought bubble reading 'DROP OR NOT?'. It carries no data; the 40% / 5% / 10% figures are all in the passage. Not attached. Page idx 23 (an ENGLISH-ONLY page — the whole of Q38 sits there).
